lesson.title: Fragmentation: Splitting a Packet to Fit the Link
lesson.summary: IP fragmentation breaks a packet that is too large for an outgoing link into smaller pieces, each carrying an offset and a flag that record exactly where its data belongs, so the pieces can eventually be reassembled into the original packet.
lesson.body:
Every link a packet crosses has a maximum transmission unit, or MTU, the largest amount of data it can carry in a single frame. A standard Ethernet link, for example, typically caps this at 1500 bytes. A packet does not always fit inside the MTU of every link it happens to cross, particularly if it originated on a link with a larger MTU or was built without regard for what lies ahead. When a packet is too big for the next link, something has to give, and IP's answer to that problem is fragmentation: splitting the packet into several smaller pieces, each of which does fit, and marking each piece with enough information to be reassembled correctly later.

Fragmentation relies on three fields already present in the IP header. The Identification field is copied unchanged into every fragment produced from the same original packet, so the receiving end can tell which fragments belong together. The Fragment Offset field records, in units of eight bytes, where within the original packet's payload this particular fragment's data starts, which lets fragments be reassembled in the right order even if they arrive out of order. The More Fragments flag is set to one on every fragment except the last, which carries it set to zero, telling the receiving end when it has reached the end of the sequence. There is also a Don't Fragment flag a sender can set to forbid fragmentation entirely, in which case a router that cannot forward an oversized packet drops it and sends back an ICMP message reporting that fragmentation would have been needed, rather than fragmenting it.

Suppose a 4000 byte IP packet, 20 bytes of header plus 3980 bytes of payload, needs to cross a link whose MTU is 1500 bytes. Each fragment needs its own 20 byte header, leaving 1480 bytes of payload per fragment, which happens to divide evenly by eight, the unit fragment offset is measured in. The first fragment carries offset 0, 1480 bytes of payload, and More Fragments set to one. The second fragment carries offset 185, which is 1480 divided by eight, another 1480 bytes of payload, and More Fragments still set to one. The third fragment carries offset 370, which is 2960 divided by eight, the remaining 1020 bytes of payload, and More Fragments set to zero, marking it as the last piece.

IPv4 allows both the originating host and any router along the path to perform this splitting, but IPv6 handles it differently and more strictly: only the originating host is allowed to fragment a packet, using a dedicated fragment extension header to carry the same kind of offset and more fragments information, while an IPv6 router that receives a packet too large for the next link simply drops it and reports back with an ICMPv6 packet too big message instead of fragmenting it itself. Either way, fragmentation only splits a packet apart. Putting it back together again is a separate job, handled entirely at the final destination, which is exactly what the next chapter covers.
